title: Recalibrating Africa’s green hydrogen strategy, Part 4
body:
Most conversations about Africa’s green hydrogen (H2) future start (and end) with the same question: Where can Africa produce H2 cheapest? This question is predominantly guided by an "export-only hydrogen economy" logic.

In earlier policy insights, I’ve argued that Africa’s H2 opportunity is bigger than this. Those insights focused largely on how African countries can expand value capture by integrating H2 into downstream activities to produce green products like green fertilizers and green steel.

But the H2 economy is not only about molecules and downstream products. It is also about machines like electrolyzers, fuel cell membranes and catalysts, precision-engineered storage tanks, and power electronics

So, the more strategic question becomes: Can African countries enter the manufacturing value chain of H2 technologies themselves?

Why does this matter?

- H2 technologies are high-value, knowledge-intensive industries and the global value chains are still forming, creating a window for technology-based industrialization.
- Technology production confers geopolitical leverage, while reducing technological dependence that may even adversely affect an export-only or domestic-industrial integration H2 model. It also generates positive externalities like skilled jobs, innovation ecosystems and emergence of adjacent sectors.

A technology-based H2 economy model in Africa is not unrealistic. What it requires is strategy.

- H2 demand projections (domestic + export) can be leveraged to justify localized assembly and gradual manufacturing of electrolyzers. Early-stage assembly can evolve into component manufacturing over time.
- Countries with metal fabrication industries can diversify into precision-engineered storage tanks and pressure vessels. Chemical and materials research institutions can focus on membranes and catalysts.
- Africa holds PGM critical for certain electrolyzer and fuel cell technologies. This can be leveraged.
- Governments can align public procurement and industrial policy, where support for H2 projects include local manufacturing and supplier development thresholds tied to capability upgrading.

Integrating into H2 technology value chains is about positioning

- If Africa only produces H2 using imported technology, it captures energy rents. If it integrates the resource into downstream segments, it gains industrial value. In both cases, however, it is vulnerable to geopolitics
- But if Africa participates in manufacturing the technologies that power H2 systems, it gains all—plus geopolitical leverage.

This is the difference between being a supplier or technology dependent in the H2 economy and being a power within it.

Africa’s H2 strategy should therefore be built on 3 pillars: Energy production. Industrial integration. Technology participation.
